The test image shows a **stem** at a branch junction with dense dark gray-black powdery/dusty coating, some white mycelial growth visible underneath, and brown discoloration of the underlying stem tissue. This looks like fungal sporulation on a stem.

Top candidates: Gray_Mold, Alternaria_Black_Molds_Stem_Cankers, Sclerotinia_Timber_Rot, Rhizopus_Soft_Rots.

Now let me read one reference from each candidate.
That Gray Mold reference is microscopic - not ideal for visual comparison. Now checking Alternaria stem canker.
Alternaria shows brown canker but not the gray-black powdery coating seen in the test image. Now checking Sclerotinia.
Sclerotinia shows white mycelium with developing black sclerotia - interesting but the test image has more uniform dense dark coating. For my 4th view, let me check Gray_Mold stem at field level.

This Gray Mold reference (Bugwood_23, 1573933) is very informative - it shows the exact same setting: a **stem junction** with brown lesion and gray sporulation on tomato. The test image matches this closely in morphology and location.

**Analysis:**
- Test image: dense dark gray-black powdery/velvety coating at stem junction, with white tissue visible underneath
- Gray Mold ref (Bugwood_23): brown lesion at stem junction with light gray sporulation - same anatomical site
- Alternaria: brown canker without the gray spore mass - doesn't match
- Sclerotinia: white fluffy mycelium with developing black sclerotia - different appearance
- The test image's dense gray coating is characteristic of heavy Botrytis sporulation ("dense velvety gray-brown spore mass" from symptom description)
- Bugwood IDs 1575060 (test) and 1573933 (Gray Mold ref) are in the same numeric range, suggesting same collection

The test image strongly matches Gray_Mold, with the heavier/darker sporulation explained by high humidity conditions.
